clips.title: What are Golden Datasets? (And Why You Need One for AI Testing)
clips.why: A short, clear answer to the question this lesson starts with: how do you test an AI whose answer is different every time?
look: Listen for what a golden dataset is, and who defines it.
Watch for how he judges an answer that is different every time, and compare it with a golden comment, which says what a reviewer should have said.
Ask yourself where Byte is today: answers checked by eye, or a repeatable test?
clips.after: BYTE-GOLD is our golden dataset for Byte: 240 PRs, each with the problems a good reviewer must find, written by people who know the code.

clips.title: Evaluating SZZ Implementations Through a Developer-Informed Oracle
clips.why: A researcher explains, in about a minute, where a bug comes from and how SZZ walks back from a fix to the change that introduced it.
look: The starting point is always a bug-fixing commit, like our squash commit that closes a Bug ticket.
SZZ blames the lines the fix touched to find the bug-inducing commit.
Ask yourself why SZZ can only guess. That is why our guilds confirm every candidate.
clips.after: Our miner is a plain SZZ: blame at the fix's parent, and the PR number comes from the (#NNNN) in fcp's squash subjects.

clips.title: LLM evaluation datasets: test cases and synthetic data
clips.why: Where evaluation data comes from (real history first) and when to add made-up cases on purpose, which is what our planted bugs are.
look: Real examples from your own product are the best source; they are our real bugs from fcp's history.
Synthetic data fills the gaps real data leaves, like our planted bugs for rare bug classes.
Watch for synthetic data used to make the test more varied, next to the real examples.
clips.after: BYTE-GOLD is half history (120 real bugs) and a quarter made by hand (60 planted bugs), so rare but serious classes still get measured.

practice.q: A fix commit changed two lines in tests/projects.test.ts and one line in package-lock.json, and nothing else. What does the miner report?

options.text: The PRs that last wrote those three lines
options.why: That is what blame would say without the SKIP list. Those PRs wrote a test or a lockfile, not a product bug, so they would be wrong answers in the key.

options.text: Nothing: tests and lockfiles are skipped, because a fix there is not a bug in product code
options.why: SKIP drops these paths before blame runs. A changed test or a bumped lockfile says nothing about which product PR held a bug.

options.text: The fix PR itself, because it touched the lines
options.why: The miner blames the fix's parent, so the fix PR is never the answer. Here it never gets that far, because the files are skipped.

practice.q: Complete the severity rule labelers use for golden comments.
practice.before: If you would block the merge for it, the severity is
practice.after: ; real but not blocking is medium, and minor is low.
practice.why: Labelers and Byte use the same scale, so a matched finding can be compared by severity.

practice.q: Byte reviews the 60 clean PRs of BYTE-GOLD and leaves 15 high or medium findings in total. The bar is at most 0.2 false alarms per clean PR. Does Byte pass?

options.text: Yes, because 15 findings is far fewer than 60 PRs
options.why: The bar is per clean PR: 15 divided by 60 is 0.25, which is above 0.2.

options.text: No: 15 ÷ 60 = 0.25 false alarms per clean PR, above the bar of 0.2
options.why: Every high or medium finding on a clean PR is a false alarm. At 0.25, people would see about one false alarm in every four clean PRs, more than the one in five we accept.

options.text: It depends on how many real bugs Byte caught
options.why: The two numbers are judged separately. High recall on real bugs does not excuse noise on clean PRs, because noise is what makes people stop reading.

practice.q: What should the defect sentence in a golden comment contain?

options.text: The customer's error report from the Bug ticket, for context
options.why: Ticket text can name customers, and a model reads this file later.

options.text: What is wrong in the code and what it breaks, in a reviewer's words
options.why: That is all the scoring needs to decide whether one of Byte's findings describes the same defect.

options.text: The commit hash of the fix, so the judge can check it
options.why: The fix is what happened later; the answer key describes the defect itself.

practice.q: Put the life of one real-bug case in order.
items: A Bug ticket is closed and its fix lands on main as a squash commit
The miner blames the fix's parent and lists the introducing PR as a candidate
A guild member opens the fix, the ticket and the introducing PR and confirms the cause
They write case.json with the golden comment
One reviewer checks the batch PR in byte-gold for consistent severities
practice.why: The script only proposes; people confirm and write the answer, and one person checks that severities agree across labelers.

practice.q: Why does history alone not give a good set, so that people also plant bugs?

options.text: Real bugs are too easy for Byte
options.why: Real bugs are often the hardest cases; that is not the reason.

options.text: Some serious bug classes happened too rarely in history to measure
options.why: A missing workgroup check or a locking migration may appear once a year. Planting gives each class enough cases.

options.text: Planted bugs are cheaper to label than real ones
options.why: A planted bug takes about 20 minutes, more than a real candidate's 10.
